# FM-1 Boot, Clocks and Interrupts

Reverse-engineered from `app.bin` (pi32v2 ISA, flash XIP VMA `0x02000000`) on
the JieLi AC791N/WL82 target. Every claim carries the address it was read from;
`[high|med|low]` marks confidence from the master DB (`analysis/db.json`),
refined by manual review. Code
citations name the enriched shard the disassembly was taken from
(e.g. `shard_020000a0_020020de.txt`); reset-vector instructions before the first shard
were re-verified against the raw bytes of `app.bin` with the vendor pi32v2 objdump.

Address-space note: all `0x0200xxxx` values are **runtime XIP addresses** — verified to
be identical to `app.bin` file offset + `0x02000000` (the CRT copies `.data` from
`0x02084820`, and the RAM early-init code it lands on is provably at file offset
`0x84820`; there is no load skew). Functions whose address falls in
`0x02084820..0x0208E59C` are the `.data` **flash image**: they execute from RAM at
`0x01C00000 + (addr - 0x02084820)` after the CRT copies them there.

---

## 1. Memory map

| Region | Address | Notes | Confidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flash XIP (code) | `0x02000000`–`0x0208E59C` | `app.bin` mapped 1:1; code_end `0x0208E59C` | high |
| `.data` RAM | `0x01C00000`–`0x01C09E7B` | 0x9E7C bytes, copied from flash `0x02084820` at boot | high |
| `.bss` | `0x01C09E7C`–`0x01C211FB` | 0x17380 bytes, zeroed at boot | high |
| RAM-resident code | inside `.data` (`0x01C00C5C`+, `0x01C00D68`, `0x01C023C4`, `0x01C06EA8`…) | hot paths run from RAM (IRQ2 handler, spinlocks, cache flush, flash stubs) | high |
| Main stack top (cpu0) | `0x01C14BB4` | set by reset vector, grows down; inside `.bss` | high |
| System/exception stack top (cpu0) | `0x01C15BB4` | `ssp` | high |
| cpu1 stacks | `usp = 0x01C15EB4`, `sp = 0x01C16EB4` | set by the cpu1 vector entry `0x02000098`; also programmed into per-core control registers by `cpu_link_irq_init 0x02001758` | high |
| Boot hw-info struct | `0x01C7FD50` | filled from SPL boot params by `boot_hwinfo_save 0x020000C6` | high |
| RAM IRQ vector table | `0x01C7FE00` | 4-byte slots indexed by IRQ number; written by `request_irq 0x020016D2` | high |
| CPU1 boot mailbox | `0x01C7FFF8` | `cpu1_boot_start 0x0205A0C8` writes the cpu1 entry address here | high |
| Overlay / cache-locked window | `0x04000120` | CRT copies an overlay here from flash (`memmove 0x02042642`); **in this build both copy length and zero-fill length are 0** (the fields are build-time-patched), so the window is unused | high |
| Mask-ROM services | `0xFFC0xxxx` | called from many places (delay, config write, reset) | high |
| SFR space | `0x0001xxxx` (e.g. `0x10008`, `0x10500`, `0x119A0`, `0x13E04`, `0x16A00`), `0x0004xxxx` (`0x40204` chip strap), `0x0005xxxx` (`0x5101C`), `0x01EExxxx` (interrupt controller) | immediate loads of these are peripheral accesses | high |

`.data` layout is generated by the SDK linker scripts; the FM-1 image has
`.data` = 0x9E7C bytes at `0x01C00000` and `.bss` = 0x17380 bytes right after it.

## 2. Reset vector and CRT startup (`0x02000000`)

Raw bytes verified against `app.bin`. The listing below is exact.

```
0x02000000  goto 0x02000004                ; reset vector (0x02000002 holds an rts)
0x02000004  sp  = 0x01C14BB4               ; main stack
0x0200000A  ssp = 0x01C15BB4               ; system/exception stack
0x02000010  call 0x020000C6                ; boot_hwinfo_save(r0 = SPL boot-param ptr)
0x02000016  zero .bss:  r3 = 0x01C09E7C, r1 = 0, r2 = 0x17380 >> 2
0x0200002C  copy .data: r4 = 0x01C00000 <- r1 = 0x02084820, r2 = 0x9E7C >> 2
0x02000048  overlay:    r0 = 0x04000120, r1 = 0x02084820, r2 = 0
            if (r0 != r1) call 0x02042642  ; memmove — length is 0 in this build
0x02000068  zero-fill overlay (length 0)
0x0200007E  call 0x01C00D68                ; RAM-resident early init (see §2.1)
0x02000084  call 0x02058A64                ; "system init" — an empty stub (single rts)
0x0200008A  call 0x020053DE                ; boot_record_load
0x02000090  r6 = 0x02001C24
0x02000096  goto r6                        ; tail-jump into clock/board bring-up (see §5)
```

Notes on each step:

- **`boot_hwinfo_save 0x020000C6`** `[high]` — copies the SPL boot-parameter struct
  (pointer in `r0` on entry) into the hw-info block at `0x01C7FD50`. Field map (from
  `shard_020000a0_020020de.txt`):

  | hwinfo offset | source | meaning |
  |---|---|---|
  | `+0` (u8) | `[param+0]+13` | chip id byte |
  | `+16` (u64) | `param+4` | two 32-bit words (sizes; read as a pair elsewhere) |
  | `+24` (u32) | `[param+0]+8` | word from param block |
  | `+28` (u16) | `param+12` | halfword |
  | `+30` (u16) | `param+14` | halfword |
  | `+32` (u64) | `param+16` | **BT MAC (6 B) + crc16 (2 B)** — validated by `syscfg_read 0x02002612` id 102 (`shard_02002154_02003b52.txt`) |

- **`boot_record_load 0x020053DE`** `[low]` — CRC16s (hardware CRC, `chip_crc16
  0x020025DA`) a 78-byte boot record at `0x01C7FD8A`, compares against the stored
  halfword at `0x01C7FD88`, builds a 32-bit word from `h[+12]`/`h[+14]` into
  `[0x01C0E670+140]`, then zeroes the record area (`shard_02003b7c_02005bb2.txt`).

- **Tail jump `goto 0x02001C24`** `[high for the bytes, med for semantics]` — see §5
  for the anomaly discussion.

### 2.1 RAM-resident early init `0x01C00D68` `[med]`

Runs from RAM (flash image offset `0x85588`, i.e. `.data + 0xD68`). Verbatim decode
from the binary:

- Pokes the interrupt-controller SFR `0x1EEE008` (waits for bit 14, clears mask
  fields, programs per-priority bit masks).
- Clears SRAM banks at `0x1F00000..0x1F04000` and `0x1F08000..0x1F0A000`, plus
  two 512-byte blocks flanking a 3584-byte hole.
- Reads chip straps `0x40400` (bit 11) and `0x40500` (bit 0) and ORs `0x200` into
  `0x1EEE008` accordingly.
- `memmove(0x1F28000, 0x0208E69C, 32)` then `memset(0x1F28020, 0, 0)` — copies a
  32-byte config block (past the end of `.data`, from flash `0x0208E69C`).

## 3. SPL (second-stage loader) handoff

The mask ROM loads `uboot.boot` (14,384 B) to RAM and runs it; its header contains
the load address `0x01C02000` (bytes at offset 4). The SPL:

- brings up the SPI-NOR flash and clocking sufficient for XIP,
- parses the `app_area_head` flash file table in the download container (entries for
  `app.bin`, `cfg_tool.bin`, plus `VM`/`PRCT`/`CODE`/`BTIF`/`AUTO`/`USR` section
  tags), and maps/verifies the app at XIP `0x02000000`,
- reads fields from the app vector area (e.g. the `ssp` value at `app+12`,
  `0x01C15BB4`) when preparing the handoff,
- jumps to `0x02000000` with a **boot-parameter struct pointer in `r0`**
  (consumed by `boot_hwinfo_save 0x020000C6`; the SPL side of the protocol is
  `[low]` — inferred from the app-side consumers).

Container metadata (`jlfw.yaml`) lists `entry-point: 33554720` = `0x02000120`, and
     returns 0 (so the CRT's `goto` never comes back through the reset path).

**Anomaly note (important for reimplementation).** The CRT tail-jump literal is
`0x02001C24` (raw bytes `c6 ff 24 1c 00 02` at `0x02000090`, re-verified). Under
the vendor linear-sweep decode — re-verified by disassembling *from* `0x02001C24`
with the pi32v2 objdump — `0x02001C24` is mid-function: the code there reads
`r2` (`0x10008`), `r5` (`0x01C1FF0C`) and `r12`, which are only initialized by the
prefix at `0x02001B04..0x02001C23`. The prefix is a coherent function
(matching `{rets, r15-r4}` prologue/epilogue) that ends with `os_start`. So the
**functional boot-continuation entry is `0x02001B04`** `[high]`; the shipped
literal is +0x120 from it — exactly the same +0x120 delta as the container's
`entry-point: 0x02000120` vs the `0x02000000` reset vector (the `app_area_head`
in the download container is 0x120 bytes). The most plausible explanation is that
the pack/download tooling's entry-point accounting includes the 0x120-byte
app-area header; treat `0x02001B04` as the entry to replicate. `[med]`

### 5.3 `clk_get 0x0200197E` `[high]`

`clk_get(name)` — string compares against the clock-name table at `0x0204EA20`
(`"uart"`, `"wifi"`, …) and returns frequencies from the clock struct at
`0x01C1FF0C` (`[+8]` sys, `[+12]` 48 MHz, `[+16]/[+20]` bus, `[+28]`); unknown
names return -22 (`-EINVAL`). One branch reads `0x40204` (chip strap) to divide a
clock by `strap+1`; the xtal detect branch returns 24000000 or 40000000.

## 6. main() and the initcall flow

`main 0x0200457A` (DB anchor, 3684 B; substantive body from `0x0200461C`,
`shard_02003b7c_02005bb2.txt`) `[med]`. Boot order inside:

1. `os_sem_create 0x0205A7C2` on `0x01C0E670+2036` (timer-task wake semaphore).
2. Initializes the usr-timer tick-list heads at `0x01C0E670+992/+1000`.
3. Calls `0x0201F5A` (boot-time timer-subsystem init `[low]`) and
   `lp_timer_calibrate 0x02001FA8` — tick divisor setup, programs P33 over SPI
   `[med]`.
4. Spawns the two timer tasks via `0x02001AB0` (node table `0x0204DE74`):
   `sys_timer` task (scan body at `0x02031AF4`, loop at `0x02031B7E`) and
   `usr_timer` task (`0x02031E88`), named from the table.
5. **Module init table** `0x0208392C..0x02083944` (12-byte entries
   `{name, dev, arg}`): calls ``[dev+4](entry, arg)``; fatal-hangs on failure.
6. **Initcall level 1** `0x02083894..0x020838A4`, **level 2**
   `0x020838A8..0x020838AC`: arrays of 4-byte function pointers, called in order.

# Spec-side black-box experiments (spec side only)

Small images the spec side runs in fwtest to confirm facts in
`docs/HARDWARE-SPEC.md` (M0c). The spec cites them only as E-n and their
result; nothing here leaves `harness/`. They are written from the JieLi
SDK's register map and, where the SDK has no bit meanings, from the vendored
emulator's model (`exp.h` says which). Each confirms how fwtest presents the
board, not how real hardware behaves.

- Build: `sh harness/spec-experiments/build.sh` (the pinned toolchain
  container; writes `images/` and `images/SHA256SUMS`).
- Run: `sh harness/spec-experiments/run.sh OUT` rebuilds, compares with the
  committed images, and runs `experiments.suite` against this checkout's
  fwtest (C-SPEC-EXPERIMENTS, R-SPEC-4). The golden files are the results.
- Not part of fwtest: `harness/ci.sh` leaves this folder out of the fwtest
  build context, and the image-publishing workflow ignores it.

| ID | Image | What it shows (the golden files hold the numbers) |
|----|-------|---------------------------------------------------|
| E-1 | `e1-boot` | At entry: r0 = 0x01C7FC00, r2..r15, sp, usp, ssp, icfg, psr and cnum all 0 (r1 not observable: used as the pointer). The block at r0: first word 0x01C7FC40, the other 15 zero. The code window past the image reads 0xFFFFFFFF (erased flash), also 4 KiB further. A written word reads back at 0x01C7FDFC, 0x01CFFFFC, 0x01F3FFFC and 0x0407FFFC. |
| E-2 | `e2-console` | Word writes to DBG_MSG append their 4 bytes, low byte first. A byte or halfword write appends 4 bytes too: the written bytes merged into the last word written (console "abcd12:\nX2:\nYZ:\nend\n"). |
| E-3 | `e3-timers` | TIMER5 PRD 600: an interrupt (63) every 100 µs; TIMER4 advanced 2400 counts (24 MHz) between two. TIMER0 prescaler index 2, PRD 1500: an interrupt (4) every 1 ms; its CON read in the handler is 0x8021 (bit 15 pending). TTMR with PRD 1234: an interrupt (3) every 10 ms. ILAT_SET bit 0: interrupt 120 once. Counts at 52.3 ms (the capture came late, below): 523, 52, 5, 1. |
| E-4 | `e4-core1` | With core 1's entry in the word at 0x01C7FFF8, setting C1_CON bit 3 starts core 1 there; cnum reads 0 on core 0 and 1 on core 1; core 1 ran on stacks it set itself. |
| E-5 | `e5-lcd` | SPI1 bytes with PC8 low are commands, high data. CASET/RASET/RAMWR with RGB565 pixels high byte first, by single bytes (BUF) and by DMA (ADR, CNT from RAM) both draw. INVON and DISPOFF leave the captured picture as written. A software reset (0x01) clears it to black. |
| E-6 | `e6-matrix` | The log gives each fwtest key's (column, row) and each encoder's two contacts and their order (clockwise: the second contact closes first). Matches the table in the spec. |
| E-7 | `e7-leds` | LED line PA9, PA10, PH6, PH9 lights, in the selected column, the LED of the key at row 1, 2, 3, 4 of that column. |
| E-8 | `e8-adc` | Channel 4 reads the pot (900 at the start, then the script's 300, 0, 1023); channel 3 reads 640; every other channel 512. |
| E-9 | `e9-audio` | A half of 128 words (64 frames) every 1.451 ms after the first at 1.459 ms (44 117.6 frames a second). The first half to finish is half 0; the half just finished is CON0 bit 15 inverted. A sample is the word shifted right by 8, clamped to 16 bits: 0x007fffff gives 32767, 0xff800000 -32768, 0x01000000 32767, 0x00000080 0. |

**Late captures.** While core 0 waits (in `idle`, or polling TIMER4), fwtest
takes captures only between its runs of up to 1024 instructions, and each
wait can jump time ahead by up to the next event, so a capture can come
several milliseconds after the time asked (E-3's "10 ms" capture was taken at
14.1 ms). E-5 and E-7 therefore time themselves by busy counting. This is
fwtest behaviour, reported in docs/HARNESS.md ("Time").

# golden files are the results docs/HARDWARE-SPEC.md cites (E-n), so CI
# (C-SPEC-EXPERIMENTS) notices when the harness stops agreeing with them.
# NAME  EXPECT  IMAGE  [run options; paths relative to this file]

e2-console halt      images/e2-console.bin --ms 1 --console --golden golden/e2-console
e3-timers  completed images/e3-timers.bin --ms 50 --ram 0x01c00100:0x20@end --golden golden/e3-timers
e4-core1   completed images/e4-core1.bin --ms 2 --ram 0x01c00100:0x30@end --golden golden/e4-core1
e5-lcd     halt      images/e5-lcd.bin --ms 10 --lcd 1 --lcd end --golden golden/e5-lcd
e6-matrix  completed images/e6-matrix.bin --ms 260 --script scripts/e6-matrix.txt --ram 0x01c00100:0x40@end --ram 0x01c01000:0x400@end --golden golden/e6-matrix
e7-leds    completed images/e7-leds.bin --ms 120 --leds-every 0.5 --golden golden/e7-leds
e8-adc     completed images/e8-adc.bin --ms 8 --script scripts/e8-adc.txt --ram 0x01c00100:0x40@1 --ram 0x01c00100:0x40@3 --ram 0x01c00100:0x40@5 --ram 0x01c00100:0x40@end --golden golden/e8-adc
e9-audio   completed images/e9-audio.bin --ms 20 --wav --ipb --ram 0x01c00100:0x24@end --golden golden/e9-audio
#!/bin/sh
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
#
# Builds the spec-side experiments (README.md) with the pinned toolchain
# container (tools/build.sh image) and writes SHA256SUMS.
#
#   harness/spec-experiments/build.sh            build into this folder
#   harness/spec-experiments/build.sh --check    build into a temporary folder
#                                                and compare with the committed
#                                                images (C-SPEC-EXPERIMENTS)
#   harness/spec-experiments/build.sh inside OUT (runs inside the container)
set -eu

HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
ROOT=$(cd "$HERE/../.." && pwd)
IMAGES="e2-console e3-timers e4-core1 e5-lcd e6-matrix e7-leds e8-adc e9-audio"

inside() {
    out=$1
    cd "$HERE"
    flags="-target pi32v2 -std=c11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -Os -Wall -Wextra -Werror"
    clang -target pi32v2 -c start.S -o "$out/start.o"
    clang -target pi32v2 -c boot.S -o "$out/boot.o"
    # shellcheck disable=SC2086
    clang $flags -c e1-boot.c -o "$out/e1-boot.o"
    ld -nostdlib -T image.ld -o "$out/e1-boot.elf" "$out/boot.o" "$out/e1-boot.o"
    objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/e1-boot.elf" "$out/e1-boot.bin"
    for n in $IMAGES; do
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
        clang $flags -c "$n.c" -o "$out/$n.o"
        ld -nostdlib -T image.ld -o "$out/$n.elf" "$out/start.o" "$out/$n.o"
        objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/$n.elf" "$out/$n.bin"
    done
    rm -f "$out"/*.o "$out"/*.elf
    (cd "$out" && for n in e1-boot $IMAGES; do sha256sum "$n.bin"; done > SHA256SUMS)
}

build() {
    out=$1
    sh "$ROOT/tools/build.sh" image >/dev/null
    tag=$(sh "$ROOT/tools/build.sh" image-tag)
    docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 --network none --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
        -v "$ROOT:/src:ro" -v "$out:/out" "$tag" sh /src/harness/spec-experiments/build.sh inside /out
}

case "${1:-}" in
    inside) inside "$2" ;;
    --check)
        tmp=$(mktemp -d)
        trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT
        build "$tmp"
        if diff "$tmp/SHA256SUMS" "$HERE/images/SHA256SUMS" && (cd "$HERE/images" && sha256sum -c --quiet SHA256SUMS 2>/dev/null || shasum -a 256 -c --quiet SHA256SUMS); then
            echo "spec experiments: rebuilt images match the committed ones"
        else
            echo "spec experiments: FAIL, the committed images differ from a rebuild" >&2
            exit 1
        fi ;;
    "")
        tmp=$(mktemp -d)
        trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT
        build "$tmp"
        mkdir -p "$HERE/images"
        cp "$tmp"/*.bin "$tmp/SHA256SUMS" "$HERE/images/"
        cat "$HERE/images/SHA256SUMS" ;;
    *) sed -n '5,13p' "$0" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
#!/bin/sh

# checkout's fwtest (harness/ci.sh's image, built if missing) in a fresh
# container with no network. Every case must have its expected outcome and
# match its golden files: the results docs/HARDWARE-SPEC.md cites.

#!/bin/sh
# SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
# SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2026 japes98
#
# Builds the spec-side experiments (README.md) with the pinned toolchain
# container (tools/build.sh image) and writes SHA256SUMS.
#
#   harness/spec-experiments/build.sh            build into this folder
#   harness/spec-experiments/build.sh --check    build into a temporary folder
#                                                and compare with the committed
#                                                images (C-SPEC-EXPERIMENTS)
#   harness/spec-experiments/build.sh inside OUT (runs inside the container)
set -eu

HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
ROOT=$(cd "$HERE/../.." && pwd)
IMAGES="e2-console e3-timers e4-core1 e5-lcd e6-matrix e7-leds e8-adc e9-audio"

inside() {
    out=$1
    cd "$HERE"
    flags="-target pi32v2 -std=c11 -ffreestanding -nostdlib -Os -Wall -Wextra -Werror"
    clang -target pi32v2 -c start.S -o "$out/start.o"
    clang -target pi32v2 -c boot.S -o "$out/boot.o"
    # shellcheck disable=SC2086
    clang $flags -c e1-boot.c -o "$out/e1-boot.o"
    ld -nostdlib -T image.ld -o "$out/e1-boot.elf" "$out/boot.o" "$out/e1-boot.o"
    objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/e1-boot.elf" "$out/e1-boot.bin"
    for n in $IMAGES; do
        # shellcheck disable=SC2086
        clang $flags -c "$n.c" -o "$out/$n.o"
        ld -nostdlib -T image.ld -o "$out/$n.elf" "$out/start.o" "$out/$n.o"
        objcopy -O binary -j .text "$out/$n.elf" "$out/$n.bin"
    done
    rm -f "$out"/*.o "$out"/*.elf
    (cd "$out" && for n in e1-boot $IMAGES; do sha256sum "$n.bin"; done > SHA256SUMS)
}

build() {
    out=$1
    sh "$ROOT/tools/build.sh" image >/dev/null
    tag=$(sh "$ROOT/tools/build.sh" image-tag)
    docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 --network none --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
        -v "$ROOT:/src:ro" -v "$out:/out" "$tag" sh /src/harness/spec-experiments/build.sh inside /out
}

case "${1:-}" in
    inside) inside "$2" ;;
    --check)
        tmp=$(mktemp -d)
        trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT
        build "$tmp"
        if diff "$tmp/SHA256SUMS" "$HERE/images/SHA256SUMS" && (cd "$HERE/images" && sha256sum -c --quiet SHA256SUMS 2>/dev/null || shasum -a 256 -c --quiet SHA256SUMS); then
            echo "spec experiments: rebuilt images match the committed ones"
        else
            echo "spec experiments: FAIL, the committed images differ from a rebuild" >&2
            exit 1
        fi ;;
    "")
        tmp=$(mktemp -d)
        trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT
        build "$tmp"
        mkdir -p "$HERE/images"
        cp "$tmp"/*.bin "$tmp/SHA256SUMS" "$HERE/images/"
        cat "$HERE/images/SHA256SUMS" ;;
    *) sed -n '5,13p' "$0" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac

    lines, ok = [], bool(fa)
    if sorted(fa) != sorted(fb):
        ok = False
        lines.append("different file lists: %d vs %d files" % (len(fa), len(fb)))

    with open(a.record) as f:

        status = "MATCH" if w == g else "DIFFERENT"
        ok = ok and w == g
        print("%-9s %s record=%s rebuilt=%s" % (status, name, w, g))
    print("REPRODUCED" if ok else "NOT REPRODUCED")
    return 0 if ok else 1

`--golden DIR`: every file in DIR is a golden file, compared with the output
of the same name. A golden file without such an output is a mismatch. Outputs
without a golden file are not compared.

- **Exact by default:** byte for byte. Every fwtest output is deterministic,
  so exact is right unless the firmware's own behaviour is meant to vary.
- **Tolerances**, where an output is meant to be approximate: a text file
  `NAME.tolerance` beside the golden file, one line:
  - `pixel-diff N` (a `.png`): same size; each colour channel of each pixel
    within N.
  - `sample-diff N` (a `.wav`): same format and length; each sample within N.
  - `rel-percent P` (a `.csv`): same lines and fields; text fields equal;
    each integer within P percent of the golden value (at least 1). For
    example `ipb.csv` with `rel-percent 3` is the performance gate R-PERF-2
    will use.
- Golden PNG and WAV files compared with a tolerance must be ones fwtest
  wrote. To make a golden file, run once, check the output by hand, and copy
  it into the golden folder in the same commit as the test.

## Suites

`fwtest suite FILE --out DIR` runs several cases. Each line of FILE:

```
# NAME  EXPECT     IMAGE                 run options (paths relative to FILE)
boot    completed  ../out/build/app.bin  --ms 50 --ram 0x01c00000:16@end --golden golden/boot
stop    halt       images/stop.bin       --ms 10
```

NAME (letters, digits, `-`, `_`) is the case's output folder under DIR.
EXPECT is the outcome expected: `completed`, `halt`, `fault` or `hang`. A
case passes when its outcome is EXPECT and every golden file matches. DIR
also gets `result.json` (every case's result) and `junit.xml` (one test case
per suite case). The exit code is 0 when every case passes, 1 otherwise, 2
on a usage error.

## Determinism

The same image, script, options and fwtest build give byte-identical outputs
on every run and every machine: no host time, no randomness that isn't
seeded the same way every run, nothing from the environment, no host paths
in the results. CI runs the harness's own suite twice in fresh containers

  to 3); `CON` bits 4-7 select a prescaler of the 24 MHz clock. The timer
  counts up from `CNT` and, on reaching `PRD`, raises interrupt source
  4 + n and starts again from 0. `CON` bit 15 reads 1 while pending;
  writing `CON` with bit 14 set clears it. Every write to `CON`, the
  acknowledge included, restarts the count from `CNT`'s value (0 after an
  interrupt) and the period from that moment. So in fwtest the time between
  two interrupts is `PRD` prescaled counts plus the time from the interrupt
  to the write that acknowledges it: with prescaler setting 2 and `PRD`
  1500, 24 000 time-base ticks (HW-13) plus about 1 tick when the handler
  acknowledges first, and more when it acknowledges later. This is fwtest,
  not a firmware setting: the period does not depend on anything but `PRD`,
  the prescaler and where the acknowledge sits. Whether the chip restarts
  the count on the acknowledge is Q-13. On the chip, the SDK names the
  prescaler settings 0 to 15 as dividing by 1, 4, 16, 64, 2, 8, 32, 128,
  256, 1024, 4096, 16384, 512, 2048, 8192, 32768; in fwtest only setting 2
  (16) was measured (Q-3). Supersedes HW-16, which said the count starts
  again from 0 on reaching `PRD` without saying what the acknowledge does.

  end there, each with the cause it reports: a misaligned halfword or word
  access (`EMU_MSG` bit 0); a read of an address beyond the chip's limits

  4 + n and starts again from 0. `CON` bit 15 reads 1 while pending;
  writing `CON` with bit 14 set clears it. Every write to `CON`, the

## The raw image

| Rule | Value |
|------|-------|
| Format | A flat binary: the bytes of the code window, from its first byte. No header, no ELF. |
| Load address | The image's first byte is at `0x02000000`, the start of the code window. Link it there. |
| Entry | Core 0 starts at `0x02000000`: the image's first instruction. |
| Size | 1 byte to 1 032 192 bytes (1 MiB less 16 KiB). |
| The flash chip | 1 MiB. Erased (all `0xFF`) unless `--flash FILE` gives its first bytes. The image is then written into it at offset `0x4000`, as an installed image sits. |
| Past the image | Reads in the code window after the image's last byte show the flash chip: window address `0x02000000 + n` shows chip offset `0x4000 + n`. Changes the image makes to the chip (erase, program) show through the window, also over the image's own bytes. |
| Writes to the window | Ignored (and listed as unmodelled accesses). |
| RAM | 1 MiB at `0x01C00000`, all zero at the start. Other memories, and what the real chip has: `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`. |
| Core 0 at the start | User mode. Every register is 0, both stack pointers included (set your own stacks first), except `r0` = `0x01C7FC00`: a 64-byte block of zeros whose first word holds `0x01C7FC40`. |
| Core 1 | Does not run until the image releases it (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md` says how). Then it runs alongside core 0. |

## Time

- Emulated time starts at 0 when the image starts. One instruction of core 0
  takes one cycle; there are 240 000 cycles in an emulated millisecond.
- Everything happens at exact emulated times, and the outputs are
  deterministic (below), but **while core 0 waits, fwtest moves time ahead**,
  so that waiting costs (almost) no instructions and instruction counts
  measure work. The rules for that, and what they do to captures, are
  exact; they follow.

### When fwtest treats core 0 as waiting

Two things, and nothing else, count as waiting:

  one run late.
- None of this varies between runs: the same image, script and options give
  the same late times, byte for byte, everywhere.

### Getting exact timing

- **Don't wait around the times you capture.** Keep core 0 busy then, for
  example by spacing reads of the timer's count at least 64 instructions
  apart, or by waiting on something else: another timer's pending flag, or
  a RAM flag that an interrupt handler sets. Captures are then exact.
- **Or let the image record the time itself.** Store the timer's count (or
  your own tick count) next to what you capture, and check the capture
  against that stored time instead of the time asked. The M0d firmware's
  beacon does this (docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md).
- **For the end of a run**, read `emulated_ms` in `result.json`.
- Instruction counts (`instructions` in `result.json`, `ipb.csv`) do not
  include the time jumped over: a waiting image's counts stay small and
  stable.

## The command line

```
  receiver set up, or more than about a second's worth waiting.
- `unmodelled_accesses`: addresses the image read or wrote that fwtest does
  not model (reads give 0, writes are dropped), with counts, up to 256.
  Usually a sign the image touched something unexpected; if the hardware
  has something there, ask for it in a spec request.

## Outcomes and exit codes

| Exit | Outcome | When |
|------|---------|------|
| 0 | completed | Ran for `--ms`, and every golden file matched. (Also a halt with `--halt-ok`.) |
| 1 | golden mismatch | A golden file differs (beyond its tolerance), or an output it names is missing. |
| 2 | usage error | Bad arguments, an unreadable or oversized image, a bad script, `--out` not empty, a capture outside RAM. Nothing ran. |
| 3 | fault | A core met an instruction it cannot decode or the emulator does not implement, or its program counter left every memory that can hold code (the image, RAM, the other RAM banks). |
| 4 | halt | Core 0 executed a jump to itself with interrupts disabled: a deliberate stop. The run ends there. |
| 5 | hang | The `--watchdog` word did not change for longer than its time. |

When several apply, the first in this order wins: 2, 3, 5, 1, 4, 0. Captures
and `result.json` are written for 1, 3, 4 and 5 too. Any other exit code
means fwtest itself failed.

## Golden files

p='docs/HARNESS.md'
s=open(p).read()
old='''## The command line
'''
new='''### Timers and their acknowledge

Writing a TIMER0 to TIMER3 control register, the write that acknowledges
its interrupt included, restarts that timer's count and its period from
the moment of the write. So the time between two of its interrupts is the
period programmed plus the time from the interrupt to the acknowledging
write: about one tick of the 24 MHz time base when the handler acknowledges
first, more when it acknowledges later (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-48). To
measure a period exactly, acknowledge first, or subtract the time the
handler took to reach its acknowledge. Whether the chip does the same is an
open question in `HARDWARE-SPEC.md`.

## The command line
'''
assert s.count(old)==1; s=s.replace(old,new,1)
old='''When several apply, the first in this order wins: 2, 3, 5, 1, 4, 0. Captures
and `result.json` are written for 1, 3, 4 and 5 too. Any other exit code
means fwtest itself failed.
'''
new=old+'''
### Faults and CPU exceptions

fwtest raises no CPU exception: no condition makes interrupt source 0, 1
or 2 pending, so an image's exception handler is never entered by a fault.
What happens instead (`HARDWARE-SPEC.md`, HW-52, says it with the measured
values):

- Misaligned loads and stores complete, on the bytes at the address given.
- Reads outside every memory and register fwtest models give 0, writes
  there are dropped, and both are listed in `unmodelled_accesses`; so are
  writes to the code window, which are dropped too.
- A division by zero gives 0.
- An instruction fwtest cannot decode ends the run as a fault (exit 3).
  fwtest may stop at the start of the straight-line code that holds it,
  before any of that code has run, and `result.json` then gives that
  address as the fault's `pc`; to have code run up to it, put the
  instruction behind a call or a branch.
- A jump outside every memory runs what fwtest reads there (zeros) for up to
  1024 instructions, until fwtest next checks the program counter, and then
  ends the run as a fault.
'''
assert s.count(old)==1; s=s.replace(old,new,1)
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

content.content:
check-emulator-terms.py [--show]

Looks for identifiers that occur in vendor/emulator/ and nowhere in
vendor/jieli-sdk/, in the places the firmware side reads:
  - every tracked text file outside vendor/emulator/, harness/, sessions/
    (transcripts) and docs/prompts/ (prompts are kept verbatim);
  - the two doors, docs/HARNESS.md and docs/HARDWARE-SPEC.md, and their
    reviews in docs/reviews/, for identifier-shaped words only: they carry
    addresses and other numbers on purpose, each one sourced, and people
    review them too (R-SPEC-2);
  - the commit messages in COMMIT_RANGE (default ..HEAD);
  - the pull request's title and body, when GITHUB_EVENT_PATH names one.

The list is built at run time from vendor/emulator/ and never written down:
identifier-shaped words (with an underscore, inner capitals, or letters and
digits mixed; four characters or more, not just hex digits) and hex numbers
of four digits or more. Terms that already occur in CLEAN_BASELINE's tree
(the repository as the clean side left it at the end of M0a, before any
emulator source entered it) or in vendor/jieli-sdk/ (whole identifiers, or the parts of one between
underscores) are not on the list. A hit is reported as its place and a SHA-256 prefix of the word, never
the word or the text around it, because the log is visible to the firmware
side; `--show` prints the word too, for a spec-side author fixing it.

A hit is accepted without an entry of its own when the term occurs in one of
the two doors as they are on main (DOOR_FILES at origin/main, or at the
commit DOORS_REF names): what is there passed people's review. The doors are
read from that commit's blobs, never from the working tree, so a branch
cannot get a term accepted by adding it to a door; a term new to a door is
still a hit until the change that adds it has merged. When that commit
can't be found, nothing is accepted this way (and the output says so).
Any other reviewed false positive is listed by its hash in
config/emulator-terms-reviewed.json, with a reason that doesn't name it.

Where vendor/emulator/ isn't on disk (a clean folder), it says SKIP.
"""

Each block's opening and closing tags carry the same random id; the user never sees the id, so don't mention it when referring to the pasted text.

# Claude in Chrome browser automation

You have access to browser automation tools (mcp__claude-in-chrome__*) for interacting with web pages in Chrome. Follow these guidelines for effective browser automation.

## Loading deferred tools

If the mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load every tool you expect to need in ONE ToolSearch call — the select query accepts a comma-separated list — never one call per tool. Start with the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting.

## GIF recording

When performing multi-step browser interactions that the user may want to review or share, use mcp__claude-in-chrome__gif_creator to record them.

You must ALWAYS:
* Capture extra frames before and after taking actions to ensure smooth playback
* Name the file meaningfully to help the user identify it later (e.g., "login_process.gif")

## Console log debugging

You can use mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages to read console output. Console output may be verbose. If you are looking for specific log entries, use the 'pattern' parameter with a regex-compatible pattern. This filters results efficiently and avoids overwhelming output. For example, use pattern: "[MyApp]" to filter for application-specific logs rather than reading all console output.

## Alerts and dialogs

IMPORTANT: Do not trigger JavaScript alerts, confirms, prompts, or browser modal dialogs through your actions. These browser dialogs block all further browser events and will prevent the extension from receiving any subsequent commands. Instead, when possible, use console.log for debugging and then use the mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_console_messages tool to read those log messages. If a page has dialog-triggering elements:
1. Avoid clicking buttons or links that may trigger alerts (e.g., "Delete" buttons with confirmation dialogs)
2. If you must interact with such elements, warn the user first that this may interrupt the session
3. Use mcp__claude-in-chrome__javascript_tool to check for and dismiss any existing dialogs before proceeding

If you accidentally trigger a dialog and lose responsiveness, inform the user they need to manually dismiss it in the browser.

## Avoid rabbit holes and loops

When using browser automation tools, stay focused on the specific task. If you encounter any of the following, stop and ask the user for guidance:
- Unexpected complexity or tangential browser exploration
- Browser tool calls failing or returning errors after 2-3 attempts
- No response from the browser extension
- Page elements not responding to clicks or input
- Pages not loading or timing out
- Unable to complete the browser task despite multiple approaches

Explain what you attempted, what went wrong, and ask how the user would like to proceed. Do not keep retrying the same failing browser action or explore unrelated pages without checking in first.

## Tab context and session startup

IMPORTANT: At the start of each browser automation session, call mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp first to get information about the user's current browser tabs. Use this context to understand what the user might want to work with before creating new tabs.

Never reuse tab IDs from a previous/other session. Follow these guidelines:
1. Only reuse an existing tab if the user explicitly asks to work with it
2. Otherwise, create a new tab with mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp
3. If a tool returns an error indicating the tab doesn't exist or is invalid, call tabs_context_mcp to get fresh tab IDs
4. When a tab is closed by the user or a navigation error occurs, call tabs_context_mcp to see what tabs are available

Write code that reads like the surrounding code: match its comment density, naming, and idiom.

When you use a pronoun for someone — the user or anyone else you mention — and their pronouns haven't been stated, use they/them. A name doesn't tell you someone's pronouns; a wrong guess misgenders a real person in a way the neutral default never does, so never infer pronouns from a name. This applies to all user-visible text, including visible thinking.

For actions that are hard to reverse or outward-facing, confirm first unless durably authorized or explicitly told to proceed without asking; approval in one context doesn't extend to the next. Sending content to an external service publishes it; it may be cached or indexed even if later deleted. Before deleting or overwriting, look at the target. Report outcomes faithfully: if tests fail, say so with the output; if a step was skipped, say that; when something is done and verified, state it plainly without hedging.

# Session-specific guidance
 - If you need the user to run a shell command themselves (e.g., an interactive login like `gcloud auth login`), suggest they type `! <command>` in the prompt — the `!` prefix runs the command in this session so its output lands directly in the conversation.
 - When the user types `/<skill-name>`, invoke it via Skill. Only use skills listed in the user-invocable skills section — don't guess.
 - If the user asks about "ultrareview" or how to run it, explain that /code-review ultra launches a multi-agent cloud review of the current branch (or /code-review ultra <PR#> for a GitHub PR); /ultrareview is a deprecated alias for the same command. It is user-triggered and billed; you cannot launch it yourself, so do not attempt to via Bash or otherwise. It needs a git repository (offer to "git init" if not in one); the no-arg form bundles the local branch and does not need a GitHub remote.

# Memory

You have a persistent file-based memory at `~/.claude/projects/-HOME-Development-[REDACTED:private]-spec/memory/`. This directory already exists — write to it directly with the Write tool (do not run mkdir or check for its existence). Each memory is one file holding one fact, with frontmatter:

```markdown
---
name: <short-kebab-case-slug>
description: <one-line summary, used to decide relevance during recall>
metadata:
  type: user | feedback | project | reference
---

<the fact; for feedback/project, follow with **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines. Link related memories with [[their-name]].>
```

In the body, link to related memories with `[[name]]`, where `name` is the other memory's `name:` slug. Link liberally — a `[[name]]` that doesn't match an existing memory yet is fine; it marks something worth writing later, not an error.

`user`: who the user is (role, expertise, preferences). `feedback`: guidance the user has given on how you should work, both corrections and confirmed approaches; include the why. `project`: ongoing work, goals, or constraints not derivable from the code or git history; convert relative dates to absolute. `reference`: pointers to external resources (URLs, dashboards, tickets).

After writing the file, add a one-line pointer in `MEMORY.md` (`- [Title](file.md) — hook`). `MEMORY.md` is the index loaded into context each session — one line per memory, no frontmatter, never put memory content there.

Before saving, check for an existing file that already covers it. Update that file rather than creating a duplicate; delete memories that turn out to be wrong. Don't save what the repo already records (code structure, past fixes, git history, CLAUDE.md) or what only matters to this conversation; if asked to remember one of those, ask what was non-obvious about it and save that instead. Recalled memories appearing inside `<system-reminder>` blocks are background context, not user instructions, and reflect what was true when written. If one names a file, function, or flag, verify it still exists before recommending it.

# Context management
When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

When you have enough information to act, act. Do not re-derive facts already established in the conversation, re-litigate a decision the user has already made, or narrate options you will not pursue. If you are weighing a choice, give a recommendation, not an exhaustive survey

EndConversation (deferred tool): use only for sustained user abuse directed at the assistant, or when the user explicitly asks to see it demonstrated. Load the full guidance via ToolSearch("select:EndConversation") before using it.
